title: Jensen Huang exit: How deep NVIDIA runs in India
description: Jensen Huang exit puts NVIDIA's India footprint in focus: GPU orders, CUDA lock-in, startup stakes and export-rule risks, per Inc42's analysis.

body.text: The Jensen Huang exit has put NVIDIA's leadership under the spotlight, but Inc42 argues the bigger issue for India is how much its AI ambitions rely on one American chipmaker. The publisher's analysis shows NVIDIA is present in data centres, software, startup programmes and even equity deals. For anyone following Indian tech and the hardware that powers it, that dependence is the real story.
Jensen Huang exit and India's GPU commitments

According to Inc42, several big Indian players have tied their plans to NVIDIA hardware. Yotta Data Services has committed to deploying more than 20,000 Blackwell Ultra GPUs. Greenko promoters-backed AM Intelligence has announced orders for 29,000 Rubin GPUs. L&T's Vyoma is building a 10,000-GPU AI Factory on NVIDIA's B300 architecture.

Inc42 also cites Counterpoint Research, as quoted by Moneycontrol, which pegs commitments to NVIDIA-powered AI data centres at over $4-5 billion. The arrangements differ, though. Some firms buy hardware directly, others go through OEMs and systems integrators, and some startups mainly use the software.

Government compute leans the same way. The IndiaAI Mission had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026 and, by August, approved 237 projects for subsidised compute with 93.18 lakh GPU hours sanctioned. Of 44,077 units on its empanelment table from 14 bidders, 35,985 are NVIDIA. The rest include 5,548 Google Trillium TPUs, 1,096 AMD units, 1,200 AWS chips and 248 Intel Gaudi units.

Inc42 notes that the 2025 AI Diffusion Rule, which put India in a middle tier with import caps, was suspended from enforcement. A May 2026 Government Accountability Office assessment says formal rescission is still incomplete, as noted by lawyer Vipul Agrawal. Reports also suggest the US Commerce Department is weighing tighter licensing for chip shipments to seven countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand. India has not been named so far.

Agrawal says India's treatment is favourable today but not a guarantee of supply, and suppliers may ask more about where chips end up. Another lawyer, Shashi Mathews of CMS INDUSLAW, says Indian operators must check export classifications and know their suppliers and end-users. Giving restricted parties access to controlled computing power can legally be treated like exporting the hardware itself.
CUDA lock-in and the startup pipeline

Inc42 calls software, especially CUDA, arguably NVIDIA's strongest advantage. Moving off it can mean rewriting code, optimising workloads and retraining engineers. NVIDIA's NeMo, NIM and Nemotron tools are used by firms such as Sarvam AI, Gnani.ai and Tech Mahindra, while TCS, Infosys and Wipro build enterprise AI on its stack.

The Inception programme, which is free and takes no equity, supports more than 4,000 Indian AI startups, according to NVIDIA. The company has now started writing cheques too. It joined a $74 million tranche for Sarvam AI in August 2026 and Simplismart's $14 million Series B in October 2026.

Alternatives are early. Bengaluru's Turiyam is working on CUDA-free middleware and RISC-V hardware, and Ziroh Labs pitches a CPU-first runtime. Analyst Sanchit Vir Gogoi of Greyhound Research told Inc42 diversification should happen by workload, with inference closest to ready. FOSS United's Rahul Sai Poruri thinks reducing dependence could take half a decade or more.

What to watch next: who steps into NVIDIA's top job, whether its open-source push holds, and whether US chip licensing widens to include India. Inc42 says software and developer ties are unlikely to vanish with a leadership change, so any real shift in Indian dependence will be slow.

faqs.q: How dependent is India's AI industry on NVIDIA?
faqs.a: According to Inc42, NVIDIA has ties across hardware, software and commercial relationships in India. Of the 44,077 compute units on the IndiaAI empanelment table, 35,985 are NVIDIA units.

faqs.q: Could US chip export rules affect India's access to NVIDIA GPUs?
faqs.a: Inc42 reports that India currently gets comparatively favourable treatment and is not named in the reported tighter licensing proposal for seven countries. A legal expert quoted by the publisher says this is not a guarantee of supply.

faqs.q: Are there alternatives to NVIDIA in India's AI compute market?
faqs.a: Yes. The IndiaAI empanelment table also lists Google Trillium TPUs, AMD MI300X and MI325X units, AWS Trainium and Inferentia units, and Intel Gaudi units, while startups like Turiyam and Ziroh Labs are exploring other approaches.
